title: {{NAME}} and the Forgotten Garden of Gear and Light
moral: Something broken is not something lost, and the most beautiful things are often those that have been carefully tended back to life.

pages.content:
The map was pressed into the spine of a secondhand book {{NAME}} found at the market, folded so many times it had almost become part of the paper. Unfolded carefully on the kitchen table, it revealed a walled garden somewhere in the hills east of the city, labelled in faded ink simply THE QUEEN'S MECHANICAL GARDEN, and beneath that, in a different hand, abandoned.

The word abandoned had been crossed out and replaced with waiting.

The garden took three hours to find, and when {{NAME}} found it the walls were taller than he had imagined, grey stone covered so thoroughly in flowering vine that it appeared to be growing rather than built. The wooden gate had swollen shut but yielded to a firm push, and beyond it, thick with wild overgrowth, lay the most extraordinary ruin {{NAME}} had ever seen.

Metal flowers. Hundreds of them, copper and brass and tarnished silver, rising from the earth on jointed stems, their petals frozen open as though time had simply stopped while they were blooming. Among them, half-wrapped in the kind of moss that takes years to grow, were the still shapes of robots, some standing, some seated on stone benches, all motionless, all beautifully made.

And in the centre of the garden, her coat the pale ivory of old piano keys, stood a unicorn.

She looked at {{NAME}} as though she had been expecting him, and took one slow step forward.

pages.content:
The unicorn's name, as far as {{NAME}} could understand, was Ivory. She communicated not in words exactly, but in images that arrived in {{NAME}}'s mind fully formed, the way a dream sometimes does: vivid, complete, and gone if you didn't hold on to them quickly.

The first image was of a princess. Young, dark-haired, wearing spectacles and a crown that sat at a slight tilt from inattention. She was kneeling in the garden soil with oil on her hands, repairing the joint of a small copper rabbit.

The second image was of the princess older, leaving. A carriage. A long road. The gates closing behind her. The robots watching from their positions in the garden beds.

'She left them,' {{NAME}} said.

Ivory shook her head, sending the long ivory fall of her mane swaying. A third image: the princess's hand on the gate, her face turned back, not leaving freely but being called away, the expression of someone who intends to return and has not yet accepted that they might not be able to.

'She meant to come back,' {{NAME}} said. The weight of it settled on him, heavy and specific.

He looked around at the frozen metal flowers, the moss-covered robots. One of the robots near him, a small one built in the shape of a hedgehog, had its head turned toward the gate in a posture of unmistakable hope.

'Right,' {{NAME}} said quietly. 'Then let's get them working again.'

pages.content:
{{NAME}} did not know very much about robotics, but he knew how things worked in a general mechanical sense, from years of taking apart and reassembling anything that stood still long enough, and the robots of the Mechanical Garden turned out to be beautiful in their engineering, elegant and logical, sealed against weather by design.

Their problem was not damage. It was absence. Each robot had a small crystal receiver where a command signal would connect it to the garden's central beacon, and the beacon had stopped transmitting. The beacon was the tall copper tower at the garden's north end, weathered and silent, its cogs locked with decades of non-use.

Ivory approached the tower while {{NAME}} examined its base mechanism, and pressed her horn to the copper plating. Light ran from her horn down through the metal, warm and searching, finding the locked cogs and the seized gears and the crystal transmitter at the beacon's heart.

{{NAME}} reached into the base mechanism with both hands and freed the primary gear by feel, the way you find a stuck drawer catch in the dark. It took four attempts. On the fifth attempt, something deep inside the tower shifted.

Then the cogs moved.

Slowly at first, grinding, finding their rhythm, then more freely, and the transmitter at the beacon's heart lit up pale gold, and the crystal receivers in every robot in the garden began to glow, and the metal flowers began to open, their petals moving joint by joint, and the copper rabbit's ears rotated, and the hedgehog turned its head from the gate and looked at {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
But the largest robot did not wake.

He was seated on the stone bench nearest the garden's centre fountain, a tall and dignified figure with a carved face that suggested the patient kind of sadness, his hands resting open on his knees as though he had placed something in them for safekeeping and it had been taken away.

The other robots gathered near him. The hedgehog pressed against his foot. The copper rabbit sat between his hands. They did not push or pull. They simply stayed close, in the manner of those who know that presence is sometimes the only useful thing.

{{NAME}} sat on the bench beside him. Ivory stood before them both.

'His crystal is different,' {{NAME}} said. It was darker than the others. Not tarnished. Darker from within.

Ivory's image came: the large robot and the princess, side by side, the princess's hands in the soil and the robot beside her, handing her tools, and the specific quality of stillness between them, the kind that needs no translation.

'He's been waiting the longest,' {{NAME}} said. 'And he's been the one keeping the others company. All this time.'

He reached out and placed his hand flat on the robot's chest, the way you put your hand on a door you are about to open, and held it there. Ivory pressed her horn gently to the robot's shoulder.

The crystal, very slowly, began to lighten.

pages.content:
The garden-keeper robot opened his eyes at dusk.

They were the colour of old amber, warm and deep, and they moved first to the garden around him, taking in the open flowers and the woken robots and the evening light on the copper and brass, all of it, carefully, before settling on {{NAME}}.

He did not speak. He reached into the breast pocket of his tarnished coat and produced a small folded note, its paper aged to the colour of cream, and held it out.

{{NAME}} opened it. The handwriting was the same as the word waiting on the map. It said: I will come back. Please keep them well until I do. Thank you for reading this.

{{NAME}} folded the note and pressed it carefully back into the robot's hand. The robot closed his fingers around it.

The garden was beautiful in the evening. The metal flowers caught the last light and turned it into something that had no name except perhaps the kind of warmth you feel when something long-lost is found again.

Ivory nuzzled {{NAME}}'s shoulder, soft and insistent.

He walked home through the vine-covered gate, which closed behind him with a sound like a satisfactory conclusion, and fell asleep quickly, warmly, the map folded on his bedside table.

Because the map had two sides. He had only looked at one. And when he had glanced at the other, just before sleep, he had seen a road drawn in pencil that led, eventually, to a name.

The princess's name.
